title: Given a grid of cell heights, water can flow from a cell to a neighbor of equal or lower height. The Pacific borders the top and left edges, the Atlantic the bottom and right. Return all cells from which water can reach both oceans.
shortTitle: Pacific Atlantic Water Flow: multi-source BFS/DFS from both oceans
keyPoints: Reverse the flow: BFS or DFS inward from each ocean's border, climbing uphill to equal-or-greater neighbors
Two boolean matrices mark which cells each ocean can reach; the answer is their intersection
Seeding from borders turns per-cell outward searches into just two linear sweeps
Time is O(rows x cols) because each cell is visited at most twice, once per ocean
Space is O(rows x cols) for the two reachability matrices
The equal-or-greater comparison correctly models the reversed downhill flow

s1_definition.oneliner: Reverse the flow: BFS/DFS inward from each ocean's border going uphill, mark each ocean's reachable set, and return the cells in both sets.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Pacific Atlantic Water Flow** – find all cells in a height grid from which water can drain to both the Pacific (top and left edges) and the Atlantic (bottom and right edges).
- **Flow reversal** – instead of searching outward from every cell, reverse the direction and search inward from each ocean's border, moving only to neighbors of equal or greater height.
- **Two reachability sets** – one boolean matrix per ocean marks which cells that ocean can reach; the answer is their intersection.
- **Linear time** – each cell is visited at most twice (once per ocean), giving O(rows x cols) time.
- **Linear space** – the two boolean matrices use O(rows x cols) extra space.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine a terrain of account-balance heights at the National Bank of India, where funds drain downhill to two settlement pools. The Pacific pool touches the top and left edges, and the Atlantic pool touches the bottom and right edges. Instead of testing every cell to see if it drains to both pools, Rajesh starts at each pool's edge and climbs uphill, marking every cell that could drain into that pool. Cells marked by both climbs are the ones that feed both pools.

```text
  Grid of heights:
  ┌─────────────┐
  │  1  2  2  3 │ ← Pacific (top)
  │  3  2  3  4 │
  │  2  4  5  3 │
  │  6  7  1  4 │
  │  5  1  1  2 │ ← Atlantic (bottom)
  └─────────────┘
  ↑               ↑
  Pacific       Atlantic
  (left)        (right)

  Step 1: DFS/BFS from Pacific border (top + left)
  ┌─────────────┐
  │  P  P  P  P │
  │  P  P  P  P │
  │  P  P  P  . │
  │  P  P  .  . │
  │  P  .  .  . │
  └─────────────┘

  Step 2: DFS/BFS from Atlantic border (bottom + right)
  ┌─────────────┐
  │  .  .  .  A │
  │  .  .  A  A │
  │  .  A  A  A │
  │  A  A  A  A │
  │  A  A  A  A │
  └─────────────┘

  Step 3: Intersection (P and A)
  ┌─────────────┐
  │  .  .  .  X │
  │  .  .  X  X │
  │  .  X  X  . │
  │  X  X  .  . │
  │  X  .  .  . │
  └─────────────┘
  X = cells reaching both oceans
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Pacific Atlantic Water Flow asks which cells in a height grid can drain water to both the Pacific and Atlantic oceans. The naive approach runs a search from every cell to test both-ocean reachability, which is extremely expensive. The efficient solution reverses the flow: start from each ocean's border cells and climb uphill, moving only to neighbors of equal or greater height.

Two boolean matrices, one per ocean, mark every cell each search can reach. A marked cell means water from that cell can flow downhill back to the ocean that seeded the search. After both sweeps, the answer is every cell marked in both matrices.

The reversal of direction is the insight interviewers test. It turns per-cell outward searches into just two linear border-seeded sweeps, bringing the time from O((m*n)^2) down to O(m*n). The equal-or-greater comparison in the reversed DFS correctly models the reversed downhill flow.

In a settlement-terrain model at the National Bank of India, each cell has a height representing a balance level, and liquidity drains downhill to two settlement pools bordered by opposite edges. Finding cells that feed both pools is this exact problem, and seeding the search from each pool's border and climbing uphill computes both reachable sets in two linear passes.

Remember one sentence: reverse the flow by climbing uphill from each ocean's border, mark the two reachability sets, and return their intersection.
